rounds.proof_sketch: block_size=256 → 8 warps → warp_id ∈ [0,7]. Array accesses: writes to warp_maxs[0..7], reads from warp_maxs[0..7]. Array size 31 supports indices 0..30, so all accesses (max index 7) are in-bounds. Original[32] and Mutant[31] both satisfy index requirements.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation reduces the shared memory array size from 32 to 31 elements. However, with block_size=256 (fixed constant), there are exactly 8 warps per block, meaning warp_id ranges from 0 to 7. The maximum index accessed in warp_maxs[] is therefore 7, which is well within bounds for an array of size 31 (valid indices 0-30). Both the write operation (warp_maxs[warp_id] where warp_id ∈ [0,7]) and the read operation (warp_maxs[lane_id] where lane_id < 8) remain valid. The mutation is functionally equivalent because it doesn't affect any actual memory access patterns.
rounds.kill_strategy: This mutant is unkillable under the fixed configuration. The array size reduction from 32 to 31 has no effect because only indices 0-7 are ever accessed when block_size=256. No value-level input can change the maximum warp_id, which is determined by block_size, not input values.
rounds.recommendations: Mutation testing tools should incorporate static range analysis for array bounds mutations. When array size is reduced but all access indices are provably within the new bounds (based on fixed constants like block_size), the mutation should be flagged as potentially equivalent before expensive dynamic testing.
